# **Custom Pretraining and Fine-Tuning Methodologies in Deep Transfer Learning for Time Series**

## **Theoretical Foundations and the Deep Learning vs. Tree-Based Trade-off**

Traditional time series analysis typically operates under the assumption that historical training observations and future test series are drawn from the same stationary distribution.1 In real-world applications, such as medical diagnostics, industrial condition monitoring, and financial market tracking, this assumption is routinely violated by temporal drift, physical shifts in sensor environments, and variable operational modes.3 Rather than executing the costly and labor-intensive process of gathering and annotating large datasets for every distinct deployment environment, deep transfer learning relaxes these distribution assumptions.1 By establishing a two-stage paradigm of pretraining on a data-rich source domain and transferring the learned parameters to a target domain, transfer learning provides an effective parameter initialization that improves generalizability and sample efficiency on downstream tasks.2  
In selecting an modeling framework for sequential data, practitioners face a clear trade-off between Deep Learning (DL) models and Tree-Based Machine Learning (TBML) methods, such as LightGBM.6 Empirical evaluations highlight a divergence in performance that is highly sensitive to the methodological framing of the research.6

| Evaluation Focus | Tree-Based Performance Metric (FPA / WRA) | Deep Learning Performance Metric (FPA / WRA) | Primary Structural Characteristics & Transferability Limitations |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Deep Learning-Focused Studies** | Low (Baseline comparison) | High (+33.79% FPA / \+0.2891 WRA) | DL architectures optimize continuous temporal features; parameters are highly transferable across domain boundaries via weight initialization.2 |
| **Tree-Based Focused Studies** | High (+66.67% FPA / \+0.5694 WRA) | Low (Non-optimized structures) | TBML models rely on static tabular splits; highly efficient and robust but lack a mechanism to transfer latent representations without complete retraining.2 |
| **Balanced, Unbiased Benchmarking** | Slightly Superior (+15.23% FPA / \+0.1771 WRA) | Competitive | TBML maintains competitive baseline accuracy and computational efficiency, but remains constrained to single-domain local modeling.6 |

While tree-based models exhibit localized robustness and training speed, they are structurally incapable of representation transfer.2 Deep learning architectures, by contrast, automatically extract hierarchical spatiotemporal features from source domains.2 These pre-trained features can then be adapted to distinct targets, bypassing the need for manual feature engineering and resolving the limitations of data scarcity in specialized domains.2

### **Recurrent Network Mechanics and Gating Functions**

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) process sequences sequentially, utilizing parameter sharing across timestamps to handle variable-length inputs.9 During training, Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) computes gradients by unrolling the network across the sequence length.9 However, as the sequence length ![][image3] scales, BPTT is severely constrained by vanishing or exploding gradients, which limits the network’s capacity to learn long-term dependencies.9  
To stabilize these gradient paths, custom recurrent pretraining relies on Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) or Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) blocks.5 These architectures introduce gating mechanisms to regulate information flow.9 In a GRU block, the transition dynamics at timestamp ![][image5] are governed by the reset gate ![][image6] and the update gate ![][image7], which process the current input ![][image8] and the previous hidden state ![][image9] 9:  
![][image10]  
![][image11]  
The reset gate determines whether the past hidden state is ignored (allowing the model to drop irrelevant historic context), while the update gate dictates how much of the candidate state ![][image12] is written to the active hidden state ![][image13] 9:  
![][image14]  
![][image15]  
LSTM networks expand this gating paradigm by segregating the cell state and the hidden state, utilizing distinct forget (![][image16]), input (![][image17]), and output (![][image18]) gates to manage long-range temporal preservation.9 Chaining these gated blocks allows recurrent transfer frameworks to extract robust temporal signatures across variable horizons.5

### **Supervised Source Task Pretraining**

In supervised pretraining, a deep backbone model is trained on a labeled source dataset where annotations are plentiful.2 For Time Series Classification (TSC), a common approach is to pre-train a three-layer Fully Convolutional Network (FCN).10 The FCN architecture is constructed without down-sampling layers to preserve temporal location, and it utilizes 1D convolutional kernels followed by Global Average Pooling (GAP) and a Softmax classification head.10  
When transferring this model to a target dataset with limited labels, the GAP features are leveraged by replacing the original Softmax classifier with a target-specific output layer.10 To mitigate negative transfer and optimize the source selection process, Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) can be applied as an inter-dataset similarity metric.10 By aligning the temporal axes of different datasets, DTW measures morphological distance to predict which source domain pretraining will yield the highest target accuracy, successfully guiding transfer across diverse classification tasks.10

## **Self-Supervised Custom Pretraining Frameworks**

To leverage massive volumes of unlabeled sequential data, self-supervised pretraining utilizes auxiliary pretext tasks to build robust representations.2

### **Generative and Reconstructive Pretraining**

Generative and reconstructive pretraining forces a model to reconstruct original time series values from corrupted, compressed, or masked inputs.2 A classic sequential implementation is TimeNet, which trains a stacked GRU encoder-decoder as an autoencoder.5 By simultaneously training on multiple distinct datasets, the decoder is forced to rely entirely on a fixed-dimensional bottleneck vector ![][image19] to reconstruct the input, capturing highly generalized, multi-domain temporal abstractions.5  
For transformer-based backbones, point-level and patch-level masked autoencoding have become the primary reconstructive paradigms.2 The Ti-MAE framework randomly masks out point-level embedded time series values and optimizes a transformer encoder-decoder to reconstruct the missing values.15  
Expanding on this, patch-level masking projects local, non-overlapping temporal windows into patch tokens before masking.2 This approach reduces computational complexity and preserves local trends.2

### **Contrastive Pretraining Paradigms**

Contrastive learning operates on the principle of instance discrimination, mapping positive pairs (different augmented views of the same sequence) close together in the latent space while pushing negative pairs (views from different sequences) apart.15  
Within temporal contrastive frameworks, TS-TCC uses strong and weak augmentations to generate multi-view inputs.15 It employs a temporal contrasting module to perform cross-view predictions, alongside a contextual contrasting module to maximize mutual information across different views of the same window.15  
To extract features across multiple temporal scales, the TS2Vec framework implements hierarchical contrastive learning over augmented context views.8 The structural backbone of the TS2Vec encoder consists of an input projection layer, a random timestamp masking module, and a dilated CNN module composed of ten residual blocks.21 Each block utilizes 1D dilated convolutions with exponentially increasing dilation factors:  
![][image20]  
This design creates a wide receptive field that extracts contextual representations at multiple granularities.21  
However, because contrastive objectives focus primarily on instance discrimination rather than data distribution modeling, their learned representations can be amplitude-agnostic.8 This degradation in amplitude sensitivity can be resolved by coupling the contrastive encoder with a Phase-Amplitude Integration (PAI) diagnostic module.8 By comparing cosine and Euclidean distances in the representation bank, PAI restores amplitude sensitivity, enhancing downstream performance on amplitude-related anomaly detection.8

### **Hybrid and Co-learning Formulations**

To combine the distribution modeling of generative pretraining with the discriminative strength of contrastive methods, hybrid architectures utilize dual-loss optimization.15 The Collaborative Generative and Contrastive (CoGenT) framework utilizes multivariate patching and patch-level masking, feeding the representations into both a contrastive projection head and a reconstructive decoder.15 The model is trained using a joint objective function:  
![][image21]  
where ![][image22] is a balancing hyperparameter.15  
Similarly, Adaptive Contrastive Masked Autoencoding (AC-MAE) integrates standard masked autoencoder reconstruction with a supervised contrastive loss applied to visible tokens.14 To prevent early representation collapse, AC-MAE introduces a ramp-up schedule that dynamically increases the weight of the contrastive loss component as features mature, ensuring the model builds semantically structured representations in low-data regimes.14

## **Time-Series Domain Adaptation and Temporal Alignment under Drift**

Time-Series Domain Adaptation (TSDA) transfers knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain.4 TSDA must be systematically classified across three core dimensions: Access-Privacy Regimes, Category-Space Semantics, and Source-Target Topologies.4

| Taxonomy Axis | Classification Category | Technical Definition & Operational Parameters | Primary Domain Challenges |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Access-Privacy Regime** | Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) | Joint training with labeled source data and unlabeled target data.4 | High domain discrepancy; requires concurrent access to source and target data.4 |
|  | Source-Free Domain Adaptation (SFUDA) | Target adaptation using only a pre-trained source model, without raw source data.4 | Severe domain shift; risk of overconfident target predictions outside the source support.22 |
|  | Black-Box Domain Adaptation (BBDA) | Adaptation utilizing only target observations and predictions from a closed-source network API.4 | Limited model access; requires output-level distillation and predictive alignment.4 |
|  | Federated Domain Adaptation (FDA) | Multi-node adaptation under local data silo constraints.4 | Network latency and decentralized gradient synchronization.4 |
| **Category-Space Semantics** | Closed Domain Adaptation | Source and target domains share an identical label space (![][image23]).4 | Basic alignment of covariate shifts.4 |
|  | Partial Domain Adaptation | Target label space is a subset of the source label space (![][image24]) | Out-of-distribution source classes can degrade target feature alignment. |
|  | Open-Set Domain Adaptation (OSDA) | Target domain contains unknown classes absent from the source (![][image25]).23 | Requires identifying and isolating unknown target classes during adaptation.23 |
|  | Universal Domain Adaptation (UniDA) | No prior assumptions are made regarding the label space overlap.20 | Demands dual alignment of shared classes and isolation of private classes.20 |
| **Source-Target Topology** | Single-Source Single-Target | Direct mapping from one source domain to one target domain.4 | Simplest alignment; prone to single-source bias.4 |
|  | Multi-Source Domain Adaptation | Aggregating features from multiple labeled source domains.4 | Requires managing source conflict and balancing domain-wise contributions.23 |
|  | Multi-Target Domain Adaptation | Adapting a single source model to generalize across multiple targets.4 | Demands fair alignment to prevent performance degradation on specific target domains.4 |

### **Adversarial and Spectral Adaptation Methods**

Adversarial domain adaptation aligns feature distributions via a minimax game between a feature extractor and a domain discriminator.25 In the recurrent space, Variational Recurrent Adversarial Deep Domain Adaptation (VRADA) combines a variational recurrent neural network (VRNN) with an adversarial discriminator.24 This design allows the model to capture non-linear temporal dependencies while ensuring the extracted latent variables remain domain-invariant.24  
For convolutional backbones, CoDATS utilizes a 1D CNN feature extractor to align distributions across multi-source settings, optimizing training times compared to recurrent methods.24  
To enhance feature discriminability during adversarial training, spectral features can be integrated alongside temporal ones.26 The Adversarial CO-learning Network (ACON) addresses multi-periodicity by applying Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT) to convert raw temporal inputs into frequency representations.26 ACON utilizes a temporal-frequency domain mutual learning module where knowledge is distilled from frequency features to temporal features within the source domain, significantly enhancing the transferability of the aligned representations.26

### **Source-Free Adaptation and Uncertainty Calibration**

In source-free settings (SFUDA), direct domain alignment is challenging due to the absence of source data.4 The MAsk And imPUte (MAPU) framework addresses this by introducing an embedding-space reconstruction task.22 During target adaptation, a temporal imputer recovers randomly masked target signals within the learned embedding space, matching the temporal consistency learned by the source model.22  
However, adapting models using uncalibrated softmax outputs often leads to overconfident, erroneous predictions on target samples that fall outside the support of the source domain.22 To resolve this, Evidential-MAPU (E-MAPU) integrates evidential uncertainty estimation.22 E-MAPU utilizes this evidential uncertainty to identify target samples residing far from the source distribution, adapting the target feature extractor to map these out-of-support samples closer to the source support while keeping the classifier parameters fixed.22

## **Handling Irregularities, Varying Sampling Rates, and Missingness**

Real-world sequential data is often irregular, asynchronous, and messy.27

### **Temporal-Sampling Shifts**

"Temporal-sampling shift" occurs when the acquisition rate of the target domain diverges from that of the source domain (e.g., transitioning from high-frequency sub-Hz monitoring to low-frequency daily sampling).29 This shift violates the assumption of a fixed stride, causing severe frame-to-frame flicker and prediction instability in standard convolutional and recurrent backbones.29  
To restore temporal stability, the Time2General framework introduces a Masked Temporal Consistency Loss designed to regularize temporal prediction discrepancies across varying strides.29 By randomizing training strides, the model is exposed to diverse temporal gaps, forcing it to learn stride-invariant transition dynamics.29

### **Irregular Multivariate Time Series (IMTS)**

When data contains pervasive missingness and asynchronous observation intervals, standard grid-based convolutions fail.27 To bypass the need for uniform temporal grids, graph-based transfer learning is employed.28 The RAINDROP architecture represents every multivariate time series sample as a separate sensor graph, utilizing a temporal attention mechanism to model time-varying dependencies purely from observational data.28 RAINDROP estimates the latent sensor graph structure and leverages dynamic message passing to predict misaligned readouts and classify irregular sequences, providing a robust pathway for transferring knowledge across highly irregular sensing environments.28  
To systematically evaluate the degree of irregularity across sequential datasets, three key metrics are used:

* **Mean Inter-Observation Interval (![][image26]):** The average chronological duration elapsed between successive measurements.27  
* **Feature Observability Entropy (![][image27]):** Measures the distribution uniformity of observations across different channels.27  
* **Temporal Observability Entropy (![][image28]):** Quantifies the consistency of sampling intervals across the chronological timeline.27

| Dataset | Dimensionality (\# Features) | Mean Inter-Observation Interval (Δt) | Feature Observability Entropy (HF​) | Temporal Observability Entropy (HT​) | Principal Domain Challenges |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **GDELT** 27 | 5 | 7.2364 Hours | 1.0000 (Uniform feature logging) | 0.9964 (Highly uniform intervals) | Sparse event-based updates with long chronological intervals.27 |
| **MIMIC** 27 | 30 | 14.6157 Minutes | 0.8461 (Highly non-uniform features) | 0.6556 (Pervasive missingness) | Multi-channel clinical observations; asynchronous recording patterns.27 |
| **EPA-Air** 27 | 4 | 1.0242 Hours | 0.3777 (Sparse feature logging) | 0.9576 (Uniform intervals) | Environmental tracking; high localized missingness on specific channels.27 |

## **Custom Fine-Tuning Strategies and Post-Training Adaptations**

Following pretraining, the model’s parameters must be fine-tuned to adapt to the target domain.2 This adaptation process can be systematically classified into four distinct post-training paradigms: Supervised, Collaborative, Reinforcement, and Hybrid Fine-Tuning.30

### **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)**

Supervised fine-tuning adapts pre-trained parameters using labeled target-domain data.2 SFT is implemented via two main configurations:

* **Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning:** The pre-trained encoder weights are frozen to prevent catastrophic forgetting, and only a lightweight target classification or forecasting head (such as a ridge regression or logistic regression head) is optimized.5 This configuration is highly robust to overfitting in low-data regimes.5  
* **Full-Parameter Fine-Tuning:** The entire model, including the pre-trained encoder layers, is optimized using backpropagation on the target domain.5 While highly expressive, full-parameter SFT requires careful regularization (e.g., weight decay, early stopping) when target labels are scarce to prevent overfitting.5

### **Collaborative Fine-Tuning**

Collaborative fine-tuning coordinates parameters across multiple models or sub-networks during adaptation.30 It is categorized into three levels of integration:

* **Parameter-Level Collaboration:** Introduces regularization constraints to bind the parameters of the adapting target model to the original pre-trained source parameters, preserving generalizable feature extractors.30  
* **Model-Level Collaboration:** Employs multiple specialized sub-networks (e.g., separating seasonal and trend modeling components) that share hidden states during target adaptation.30  
* **Hybrid-Level Collaboration:** Unifies parameter-level regularization with multi-model architectural fusion.30

### **Reinforcement Fine-Tuning**

Reinforcement fine-tuning optimizes parameters using non-differentiable downstream metrics as feedback rewards.30 In multimodal tasks, this is executed by generating programmatic representations of time series.31 For example, the TS2Code framework trains models to map a time series sequence into executable Python code that reconstructs the input sequence when run.31 The reconstruction error of the executed code serves as a verifiable reward signal, allowing reinforcement learning (using algorithms like GRPO) to guide representation learning without relying on standard supervised losses.31  
These reinforcement models can be further classified by their cognitive complexity:

* **Reasoning-Driven Fine-Tuning:** Incorporates chain-of-thought pathways, prompting the network to systematically generate step-by-step mathematical reasoning steps before outputting the final sequence prediction.30  
* **Non-Reasoning Fine-Tuning:** Direct mapping of input sequences to output values, skipping intermediate reasoning chains.30

### **Hybrid Post-Training: Integrating Explicit Temporal Priors**

While self-supervised representations from models like TS2Vec excel at capturing complex, non-linear dynamics, they do not explicitly model deterministic temporal components like seasonality and trend.21 To address this structural limitation, hybrid architectures fuse pre-trained embeddings with explicit, engineered temporal priors.21  
The TS2Vec-Ensemble framework bridges this gap by passing raw observations through a dual-pathway architecture.21 The first pathway utilizes a pre-trained TS2Vec encoder to extract implicit temporal dynamics.21 The second pathway uses explicit sinusoidal regressions and statistical features to capture seasonal and periodic cycles.12  
![][image29]  
where the ensemble weights ![][image30] and ![][image31] are optimized independently for each forecast horizon ![][image32].21 This dynamic weighting scheme allows the model to prioritize short-term learned dynamics or long-term seasonal priors as needed, outperforming purely deep-learning baselines in long-horizon forecasting.21

## **Validation Methodologies and Benchmark Datasets**

Evaluating the generalization power of transfer learning models requires strict validation protocols to prevent optimistic performance bias.32 Traditional random split K-Fold cross-validation is fundamentally flawed for time series, as it violates chronological order and introduces data leakage by training on future observations to predict past states.32

### **Chronological Validation Protocols**

To evaluate the model's true generalization power under temporal drift, walk-forward validation and chronological train-validation-test splits must be enforced.32

* **Walk-Forward Validation:** Moves the training and validation windows forward through time, preserving chronological order.32  
* **Purged Group K-Fold:** Groups observations chronologically, leaving temporal gaps between folds to prevent information leakage.32  
* **Combinatorial Purged Group K-Fold:** Extends Purged K-Fold by systematically combining multiple training intervals to test performance across varied drift-aware splits.32

### **Primary Pretraining and Evaluation Benchmarks**

To establish baseline comparisons, transfer learning models are systematically benchmarked across standard clinical, financial, and physical datasets.34

| Domain / Application Area | Benchmark Dataset | Spatial & Temporal Resolution | Principal Transfer Objectives |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Point & Long-Term Forecasting** | ETT (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2) 35 | Hourly and 15-minute electricity grid metrics | Evaluating long-horizon forecasting stability and adaptation under daily load shifts.21 |
| **Short-Term & Probabilistic Forecasting** | Monash Repository Datasets 35 | High-frequency weather, demand, and transport metrics | Multi-scale pretraining; modeling parametric distributions (Gaussian, Student-t) under seasonal variance.7 |
| **Industrial Diagnostics** | M4 & M5 Competition Datasets 36 | Daily and hourly intermittent sales and retail demand | Transferring representations across hierarchical, zero-demand retail channels.41 |
| **Physiological Sensing** | DEAP / THU-EP / SEED 34 | High-frequency EEG signals (128Hz, 250Hz, 200Hz) | Domain adaptation across distinct human subjects; classifying delta, theta, and alpha bands under noisy conditions.34 |

## **Future Perspectives: Transition to Large-Scale Foundation Models**

While custom pretraining and domain adaptation enable precise control over feature representation, they require setting up dedicated upstream pipelines, locating compatible source datasets, and balancing complex multi-task losses.2 A natural progression for practitioners seeking broader generalization without custom pretraining setups is the transition to pre-trained Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs).30  
Rather than pretraining a model from scratch for a specific industrial or clinical task, TSFMs are trained on massive, heterogeneous repositories of time series (such as the Monash Time Series Forecasting Repository) and transferred zero-shot to target domains.35 Under this paradigm, lightweight, highly optimized architectures like TinyTimeMixer (TTM)—which contains fewer than one million parameters—demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance and can be fine-tuned with as little as 5% of target data.38  
For practitioners looking to scale their temporal modeling pipelines, next steps should include evaluating zero-shot capabilities and downstream adaptation strategies of prominent foundation models, such as MOMENT, Chronos, TimesFM, MOIRAI, and Lag-Llama.35 These models represent the transition from bespoke transfer learning architectures to unified, general-purpose temporal modeling systems.30
